sections.title: Introduction
sections.body: This chapter presents the practical application of shallow foundation design for bridge structures. A design process is presented in a step-by-step format that will result in a satisfactory solution for most applications of shallow foundation bridge support. The design process involves multiple engineering disciplines. The discipline generally responsible for each design step is identified, whether it be geotechnical, structural, hydraulic, environmental, or general civil. Worked foundation design examples that follow this process are included in Appendix B for spread footing support of bridge piers in the following applications: interior bridge pier supported on a spread footing founded in native soil, integral stub abutment supported on compacted structural fill, stub seat-type abutment footing supported in compacted structural fill, full-height seat abutment founded in native soil, and interior bridge pier supported on a spread footing on native rock. A discussion of the application of Load and Resistance Factor Design (LRFD) to the design of spread footings is included in Appendix C. It should be noted that these examples are intended to convey one approach and process that can lead to a satisfactory design of bridge support on a shallow foundation. The examples should not be construed as representations of the only approach that can lead to a satisfactory design. Also note that the examples only check one or, at most, a few specific load cases. In practice, every complete design should consider all applicable load cases.
key_points: Design process is multidisciplinary: geotechnical, structural, hydraulic, environmental, and general civil
Step-by-step format provided for most shallow foundation bridge support applications
Five worked design examples provided in Appendix B covering various pier and abutment configurations
LRFD application to spread footings discussed in Appendix C
Examples illustrate one acceptable approach; all applicable load cases must be checked in practice
sections.applicability: General introduction and overview of the bridge shallow foundation design process.

sections.title: Design Process and Flow Chart
sections.body: The design process of a bridge supported on shallow foundations includes the steps shown in Table 6-1 and also in the design process flow chart, Figure 6-1. The 12-step process covers: (1) developing the preliminary bridge layout (Structural), (2) reviewing existing geologic and subsurface data (Geotechnical), (3) site reconnaissance (Geotechnical), (4) determining depth of footing for scour and frost protection (Hydraulic with geotechnical input), (5) determining loads and tolerable total and differential settlement (Structural), (6) determining design soil properties from subsurface exploration and laboratory testing (Geotechnical), (7) calculating allowable bearing capacity (Geotechnical), (8) calculating allowable sliding and passive soil resistance (Geotechnical), (9) performing global stability analysis where applicable (Geotechnical), (10) sizing the footing using service loads and effective footing dimensions (Structural), (11) checking stability for sliding and overturning (Structural), and (12) completing the structural design using factored loads with trapezoidal contact pressure distribution (Structural).
key_points: 12-step design process with clear discipline assignments for each step
Steps 1-3: Preliminary layout, geologic review, and site reconnaissance
Step 4: Depth determination for scour and frost protection (hydraulic/geotechnical)
Steps 5-6: Loads, settlement criteria, soil properties from exploration and lab testing
Steps 7-9: Bearing capacity, sliding/passive resistance, global stability (geotechnical)
Steps 10-12: Footing sizing, overturning/sliding checks, structural design (structural)
Structural design (Step 12) uses factored loads and trapezoidal contact pressure, not the uniform equivalent pressure used for sizing
figures: Figure 6-1: Design Process Flow Chart - Bridge Shallow Foundation
tables: Table 6-1: Steps in Design Process for Bridge Supported on Shallow Foundations
sections.applicability: Establishing the overall design workflow and discipline responsibilities for bridge shallow foundation design.

sections.title: General Considerations
sections.body: The depth and size of a shallow foundation for support of a bridge need to be selected to ensure that the bearing materials are able to support the loads imparted without shear failure or excessive settlement. This includes verifying that the bearing materials are nonliquefiable during earthquakes. The base of the footing also needs to be below the frost depth for frost susceptible soils, and below the probable scour during a design high water extreme event.
key_points: Foundation depth and size must prevent shear failure and excessive settlement
Bearing materials must be verified as nonliquefiable during earthquakes
Base of footing must be below frost depth in frost-susceptible soils
Base of footing must be below probable scour depth during design high water event
sections.applicability: General depth and size considerations for all bridge shallow foundations.

sections.title: Scour Potential and Depth
sections.body: Scour is localized erosion of the channel bed that occurs around flow obstructions such as piers and bridge abutments, at channel contractions such as bridges, and on the outside of channel bends. It can also be the result of long-term erosion of the channel bed that can occur during a structure's life. Scour is a site-specific process that is a function of the flow velocity and duration, the geometry of the structural elements exposed to the flow of water, the geomorphology of the channel and the properties of the foundation and channel bed materials. A multidisciplinary team of hydraulic, geotechnical and structural engineers should evaluate the risk of scour-induced failure at each structure site. Scour assessment requires a determination of the cumulative effects of the three main components of scour: aggradation/degradation, contraction scour and local scour. It also requires an evaluation of potential changes in channel geometry and location that may occur during a structure's design life. Aggradation and degradation are long-term changes in the channel bed elevation caused by human activities or naturally occurring changes in basin hydrology and geology. Contraction scour is the lowering of the channel bed due to localized narrowing of a channel. Local scour occurs at bridge piers and abutments due to complex flow patterns. Scour can undermine shallow foundations or remove sufficient overburden to redistribute foundation forces causing foundation displacement and detrimental stresses to structural elements. Table 6-1 provides general guidelines for design of shallow foundations. For new structures the foundation should be designed deep enough such that scour protection is not required (Richardson & Davis, 1995).
key_points: Scour involves three components: aggradation/degradation, contraction scour, and local scour
Scour assessment requires a multidisciplinary team (hydraulic, geotechnical, structural)
Aggradation/degradation are long-term channel bed elevation changes
Contraction scour results from localized narrowing of the channel
Local scour occurs at piers and abutments due to complex flow patterns
New foundations should be designed deep enough that scour protection is not required
Channel migration potential must also be assessed over the structure's design life
Scour can undermine foundations and redistribute forces causing structural damage
sections.applicability: Assessing scour potential and determining required foundation depth at bridge waterway crossings.

sections.title: Scour Design Considerations for Shallow Foundations
sections.body: Richardson & Davis (1995) provides guidance on scour design considerations for shallow foundation support of bridges at stream crossings. For spread footings on soil: ensure that the top of the footing is below the sum of the long-term degradation, contraction scour and lateral migration (excluding local scour); place the bottom of the footing below the total scour line; the top of the footing can act as a local scour arrestor. For spread footings on rock highly resistant to scour: place the bottom of the footing directly on the cleaned rock surface for massive rock formations (such as granite); avoid small embedment (keying) since blasting frequently damages the rock structure and makes it more susceptible to scour; if footings on massive hard rock require lateral constraint, steel dowels should be drilled and grouted into the rock. For spread footings on erodible rock or IGMs: weathered or potentially erodible rock formations need careful scour assessment; the decision should be based on analysis of intact rock cores, rock quality designations and local geology. AASHTO specification requires footings for stream piers and each abutment to be founded at least 1.8 m (6 ft) below the streambed. There are four general types of scour protection: localized armoring (rock riprap, gabions, pre-cast concrete blocks, grouted riprap), river training, modifications to the foundations, and monitoring.
key_points: Footings on soil: top below degradation + contraction scour + lateral migration; bottom below total scour line
Top of footing can serve as a local scour arrestor
Footings on scour-resistant rock: place directly on cleaned rock surface; avoid keying by blasting
Footings on erodible rock/IGMs: careful scour assessment using intact rock cores and RQD
AASHTO requires stream pier/abutment footings at least 1.8 m (6 ft) below streambed
Four types of scour protection: localized armoring, river training, foundation modifications, and monitoring
Localized armoring includes rock riprap, gabions, pre-cast blocks, and grouted riprap
sections.applicability: Specific scour design guidance for spread footings on soil, resistant rock, and erodible rock at stream crossings.

sections.title: Frost Depth
sections.body: Footings founded in seasonal and permanently frozen grounds must be embedded below the depth of frost penetration (frost depth) to provide adequate frost protection. This is required to prevent heaving of the footings due to volumetric expansions of the subgrade soils from freezing and/or to prevent settling due to loss of shear strength and stiffness from thawing. In general, for frost action to occur, the following conditions must apply: presence of frost-susceptible soil, availability of water, and freezing conditions. Fine-grained soils with low cohesion tend to be more frost susceptible. Silty soil containing a high percentage of particles smaller than the No. 200 U.S. Standard sieve tends to have a network of pores and fissures that promote frost penetration. Common frost-susceptible soils include silts (ML, MH), silty sands (SM) and low-plasticity clays (CL-CL/ML). In regions where freezing of the ground occurs during winter months, lenses of clear ice will form within the fine-grained soils and result in a sequence of frozen soil and ice. If there is a source of water in liquid phase available under the frost depth, the water will be drawn toward these ice lenses by capillary and suction actions, further expanding the lenses and consequently producing surface heave. The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers proposed a relationship between frost penetration depth and the freezing index, which is a product of the number of days below freezing and the average number of degrees below freezing during the freezing season. Footings should be located below the maximum depth of frost penetration to minimize the potential for freeze/thaw movements. The maximum depth of frost penetration is generally established by local experience or from published maps. The use of generalized maps showing large regions is discouraged. Local building codes, agency design policy and experience should be consulted for appropriate design values.
key_points: Footings must be embedded below frost penetration depth to prevent heave and loss of strength
Three conditions required for frost action: frost-susceptible soil, water availability, and freezing conditions
Most frost-susceptible soils: silts (ML, MH), silty sands (SM), low-plasticity clays (CL-CL/ML)
Ice lenses form in fine-grained soils and grow via capillary suction from water below frost depth
Freezing index relates frost penetration depth to duration and severity of freezing temperatures
Use local experience or published maps for frost depth; avoid generalized large-region maps
Permafrost design is beyond scope; refer to Canadian Foundation Engineering Manual (1985)
sections.applicability: Determining required footing embedment depth for frost protection in cold climates.

sections.title: Expansive and Collapsible Soils
sections.body: Both expansive and collapsible soils are regional in occurrence. Neither soil type is well suited for shallow foundation support without some sort of mitigation for the potential for large volume changes in these soils due to changes in moisture content. Because deep foundations are frequently used for bridge support in both soil types, detailed guidance for ground treatment to permit use of shallow foundations for bridge support is not included here. Expansive clays experience increases in volume due to increases in moisture content, and the magnitude of the volume change can cause severe damage to structures. In general, deep foundations are preferred for bridge support in expansive soil terrain, unless the potential for volume change can be mitigated. The most common and effective strategy for mitigating expansion potential is to excavate and replace the expansive soil with sufficient nonexpansive material to counteract the swell potential. This is generally practical only if a ready source of nonexpansive material is located nearby. For approach embankment and abutment design, the expansion potential should be evaluated considering the construction and loads of both. Collapsible soils, when dry, can provide adequate support for relatively high loads. However, upon wetting after the load has been applied, the soils can experience dramatic decreases in volume. It is most important to identify collapse potential of foundation soils at a bridge site. Due to the difficulties in obtaining undisturbed samples of these materials, exploration and testing alone may not identify the collapse potential. Local experience and review of geologic mapping are therefore essential to identification of collapsible soil deposits.
key_points: Expansive and collapsible soils are regional in occurrence and prone to large volume changes with moisture changes
Deep foundations are generally preferred for bridges on expansive or collapsible soils
Expansive clay mitigation: excavate and replace with nonexpansive material (requires nearby source)
For approach embankments/abutments, evaluate expansion potential considering both construction and loads
Collapsible soils can support high loads when dry but experience dramatic volume decrease upon wetting
Collapse potential may not be identified by exploration and testing alone
Local experience and geologic mapping are essential for identifying collapsible soil deposits
sections.applicability: Identifying and addressing expansive and collapsible soil conditions for bridge foundation siting.

sections.title: Drainage Considerations
sections.body: When a shallow foundation supports a stemwall, and there is a difference in elevation of the backfill on either side of the stemwall so that unbalanced lateral earth pressures will act on the stemwall, the footing and the stemwall combine to function as a retaining structure. This is a typical configuration for bridge abutments. As with most retaining structures, the material retained by the structure should be drained such that hydrostatic pressures do not also act against the abutment. Abutments are important structures that perform multiple functions. Drainage details, including weep holes and perforated drainage pipes, are an essential inclusion in the plans and specifications. Most highway agencies use standard details and specifications to ensure adequate drainage behind abutments. Additional discussion of abutment and retaining wall drainage requirements and construction details are provided in Chapter 9.
key_points: Footing + stemwall with unbalanced backfill functions as a retaining structure (typical for bridge abutments)
Retained material must be drained to prevent hydrostatic pressures against the abutment
Drainage details (weep holes, perforated pipes) are essential in plans and specifications
Most highway agencies have standard drainage details and specifications for abutments
Additional drainage guidance provided in Chapter 9
sections.applicability: Drainage design for bridge abutment shallow foundations acting as retaining structures.

sections.title: Seismic Considerations and Dynamic Stability
sections.body: Seismic hazards should be assessed as part of the foundation type selection process. Shallow foundations are susceptible to excessive movements or damage if the bearing soils are subject to liquefaction or lateral spreading due to an earthquake. GEC No. 3, Geotechnical Earthquake Engineering for Highways (Kavazanjian et al., 1997), presents guidance on assessing seismic hazards at a site, including evaluation of liquefaction and lateral spreading potential. In general, shallow foundations will not be an appropriate choice for support of bridge piers when there is potential for liquefaction to develop under the design seismic event unless the liquefaction potential is mitigated by ground improvement. If liquefaction and lateral spreading are not expected at a site, shallow foundations may be a suitable and cost-effective choice for support of a bridge, provided the foundation is designed to adequately resist the seismic loading conditions appropriate for the design event. Seismic design checks should, at a minimum, include the following: (1) Design for seismic loads through the column or stemwall to the footing with a minimum factor of safety of about 1.0 to 1.15 against bearing capacity or sliding failure; (2) AASHTO (1996) permits seismic eccentricity to fall within the middle two-thirds (2/3) of the footing based on trapezoidal distribution, but this GEC recommends using rectangular pressure distribution with eccentricity kept within the middle one-half; (3) Check for seismic loads in opposite directions and for uplift; a deep foundation may be needed for uplift; (4) Design for seismic lateral earth pressures using Mononobe-Okabe equations per AASHTO (1996, 1998); (5) Check global stability of slopes supporting the footing with seismic coefficient in the slip circle, with factor of safety greater than 1.0 when the applied horizontal seismic coefficient is one-half the peak ground acceleration (Hynes-Griffin & Franklin, 1984).
key_points: Assess seismic hazards including liquefaction and lateral spreading as part of foundation type selection
Shallow foundations are generally not appropriate where liquefaction is expected unless mitigated by ground improvement
Minimum FOS of 1.0 to 1.15 for bearing capacity and sliding under seismic loads
Seismic eccentricity should be kept within the middle one-half of the footing (using rectangular pressure distribution)
Check for seismic loads acting in opposite directions and potential for uplift
Use Mononobe-Okabe equations for seismic lateral earth pressures (AASHTO 1996, 1998)
Global stability FOS > 1.0 with horizontal seismic coefficient = 0.5 * PGA (Hynes-Griffin & Franklin, 1984)
Refer to GEC No. 3 for detailed seismic hazard assessment guidance
sections.applicability: Seismic design checks for bridge shallow foundations, including liquefaction screening and dynamic stability.

sections.title: Loads
sections.body: Calculation of loads applied to shallow foundations is presented in AASHTO (1996, 1998). Numerous load groups provide for a variety of possible loading conditions and also consider the special loading requirements of non-routine structures, such as long span bridges. A summary of load cases and the conditions they are intended to check is included in Table 6-2. The designer should be aware of the possibility that a non-codified loading condition may actually control the design of a foundation. For instance, the construction sequence and methods should be considered when evaluating the critical load case for a shallow foundation. If an abutment may be fully backfilled prior to application of the superstructure loads, the overturning load of the backfill may be the most critical loading condition the foundation must ever resist.
key_points: Load calculations per AASHTO (1996, 1998) with numerous load groups for various conditions
Table 6-2 summarizes service load design load groups (Groups I through X)
Non-codified loading conditions (e.g., construction sequence) may control foundation design
Abutment backfill prior to superstructure load application can be the most critical overturning load case
Special loading requirements exist for non-routine structures such as long span bridges
tables: Table 6-2: Service Load Design Load Groups (Groups I through X)
sections.applicability: Determining design loads and critical load combinations for bridge shallow foundations.

sections.title: Vertical Loads and Pressures
sections.body: Vertical loads should be calculated in accordance with the design specification selected as the design criteria for the project. Calculation of infrequent loads, such as seismic, should consider the potential range of soil and ground water conditions that may exist under and around the footing over the life span of the structure. It is important to ensure that the structure will perform well over the range of expected conditions that may occur, considering the potential for: seasonal variations in ground water level, variation in the depth of cover over a footing due to scour or excavation, increased loads due to changes in permitted loads or the addition of overlays, and intermediate construction conditions or equipment loading that may exceed design live loads. An additional consideration related to the concept of net bearing pressure is the calculation of loads due to the self-weight of the footing and the backfill over the footing. Consider a footing constructed in an excavation below existing grade and then subsequently backfilled. The net increase in stress experienced by the soil below the bearing elevation will be due to a change in the unit weight of material replaced over the top. Because the concrete has a higher unit weight than the soil it replaces, there is a slight increase in bearing stress below the footing. For most applications, including bridge foundations, this effect is usually less than one or two percent of the loads applied by the column and is therefore commonly ignored. For mat foundations constructed well below existing grade, there may be a net decrease in stress due to the self-weight of the shallow foundation and the lack of backfill. The decision to include or ignore the effect of footing self-weight and backfill should be evaluated on a case-by-case basis considering effects on bearing stress, settlement, and eccentricity/overturning calculations.
key_points: Vertical loads per selected design specification; consider life-span range of soil and groundwater conditions
Consider seasonal groundwater variations, scour-induced cover changes, load increases, and construction loads
Net bearing pressure accounts for self-weight of footing and backfill replacing excavated soil
For spread footings, concrete replacing soil increases bearing stress by typically < 1-2% of column loads (usually ignored)
For mat foundations below grade, net stress decrease may occur due to soil removal exceeding foundation weight
Including self-weight in bearing stress is conservative; ignoring it in overturning/sliding checks is conservative
Mat foundations below grade with no backfill experience opposite effects from spread footings
sections.applicability: Computing vertical loads and net bearing pressures for bridge shallow foundation design.

sections.title: Lateral Loads and Pressures
sections.body: The transfer of shear applied by the column may apply lateral loads on a shallow foundation. The computation of these loads should be done in accordance with the appropriate section of AASHTO or the selected design criteria. For the case of abutments that retain fill, the lateral earth pressures and associated design loads must also be computed to size and design the footing. Lateral earth pressures are determined based on the characteristics of the fill material behind the abutment. The different states of stress that should be considered include active, at-rest, passive and seismic. Computation of seismic earth pressures is not included here; the reader is referred to GEC No. 3. In addition, a soil pressure distribution has to be determined for traffic surcharge. For the active, passive and at-rest states, the pressure distribution can be assumed to be triangular, with the resultant applied at H/3 from the bottom of the footing. The general equation for computing lateral loads due to lateral earth pressures is: P = (1/2) * K * gamma' * H^2 (Equation 6-1), where P is the lateral load per unit length, K is the lateral earth pressure coefficient, gamma' is the effective unit weight, and H is the height of retained backfill.
key_points: Lateral loads include column shear transfer and lateral earth pressures from retained fill (abutments)
Earth pressure states to consider: active, at-rest, passive, and seismic
Triangular pressure distribution assumed for active, passive, and at-rest states with resultant at H/3
General lateral load equation: P = (1/2) * K * gamma' * H^2
Seismic earth pressures covered in GEC No. 3
Traffic surcharge adds a uniform pressure distribution behind the wall
equations: Equation 6-1: P = (1/2) * K * gamma' * H^2 (lateral load per unit length of wall)
sections.applicability: Computing lateral loads and earth pressures on bridge abutment shallow foundations.

sections.title: Active Pressure Distribution
sections.body: The pressure distribution is determined using calculations based on Coulomb theory. The active pressure coefficient, K_a, is computed from Equation 6-2. This is the general case for Coulomb lateral earth pressure theory and does not account for surcharge or seismic loads. K_a = cos^2(phi' - theta) / {cos^2(theta) * cos(theta + delta) * [1 + sqrt(sin(phi' + delta) * sin(phi' - beta) / (cos(theta + delta) * cos(theta - beta)))]^2}, where K_a is the active earth pressure coefficient, delta is the wall/backfill interface friction angle, beta is the angle of backfill slope behind the wall to the horizontal (beta = 0 for horizontal backfill surface), theta is the angle of back wall face inclination (theta = 0 for vertical wall face), and phi' is the effective angle of internal friction for the soil. For the case of a vertical wall (no batter) and where the ground surfaces above and below the wall are level, the active pressure coefficient may be calculated using the simpler Rankine equation: K_a = tan^2(45 - phi'/2) (Equation 6-3). The Rankine equation assumes no friction between the wall and the soil backfill and does not include consideration for surcharge or seismic loads.
key_points: Coulomb active earth pressure coefficient (Equation 6-2) is the general case accounting for wall batter, backfill slope, and wall friction
Rankine equation K_a = tan^2(45 - phi'/2) is the simplified case for vertical walls with level ground
Rankine assumes no wall-soil friction; Coulomb includes interface friction angle delta
Neither Coulomb nor Rankine basic equations account for surcharge or seismic loads
Parameters: delta = wall/backfill friction angle, beta = backfill slope, theta = wall face inclination, phi' = soil friction angle
equations: Equation 6-2: K_a = cos^2(phi' - theta) / {cos^2(theta) * cos(theta + delta) * [1 + sqrt(sin(phi' + delta) * sin(phi' - beta) / (cos(theta + delta) * cos(theta - beta)))]^2} (Coulomb active earth pressure coefficient)
Equation 6-3: K_a = tan^2(45 - phi'/2) (Rankine active earth pressure coefficient)
figures: Figure 6-2: Coulomb Lateral Earth Pressure Definitions
sections.applicability: Computing active earth pressure coefficients for abutment design using Coulomb or Rankine theory.

sections.title: At-Rest Pressure Distribution
sections.body: The at-rest coefficient can be determined from the following equation developed by Mayne and Kulhawy (1982): K_o = (1 - sin(phi')) * OCR^(sin(phi')) (Equation 6-4), where K_o is the at-rest pressure coefficient, phi' is the effective angle of internal friction for the soil, and OCR is the overconsolidation (preconsolidation) ratio (see Section 5.3.3). Some agencies design abutment walls for at-rest earth pressures. However, if the wall is free to rotate such that the displacement at the top of the abutment is about 0.2 percent of the height of the wall (i.e., 0.002H), then active earth pressures can be assumed to develop.
key_points: At-rest coefficient: K_o = (1 - sin(phi')) * OCR^(sin(phi')) (Mayne and Kulhawy, 1982)
Some agencies design abutment walls for at-rest pressures as a conservative approach
Active pressures develop if wall top displacement reaches approximately 0.002H (0.2% of wall height)
OCR (overconsolidation ratio) significantly affects the at-rest coefficient
equations: Equation 6-4: K_o = (1 - sin(phi')) * OCR^(sin(phi')) (Mayne and Kulhawy at-rest coefficient)
sections.applicability: Computing at-rest earth pressure coefficient for abutment walls that do not experience sufficient rotation for active conditions.

sections.title: Passive Pressure Distribution
sections.body: The passive pressure distribution should be determined for special abutment cases. The passive pressure is generally ignored in front of the abutment due to the large lateral displacements required to fully mobilize passive lateral earth pressures and the potential for poor compaction or subsequent removal of the backfill. The passive earth pressure coefficient may be computed using Coulomb earth pressure theory or estimated from charts such as Figures 5.5.2C and 5.5.2D in the AASHTO Standard Specifications (1996).
key_points: Passive pressure generally ignored in front of abutments due to large displacement required for mobilization
Poor compaction or removal of soil in front of abutment further justifies ignoring passive pressure
When needed, passive coefficient computed via Coulomb theory or AASHTO Figures 5.5.2C and 5.5.2D
Passive pressure calculation is for special abutment cases only
sections.applicability: Determining when and how to include passive earth pressures in abutment footing design.

sections.title: Equivalent Fluid Methods
sections.body: The AASHTO Standard Specifications (1996) state that structures that resist loads due to lateral earth pressures should not be designed for less than an equivalent fluid weight of 4.8 kN/m^3 (30 pounds per cubic foot). If the above methods yield pressures lower than this equivalent fluid weight, the equivalent fluid pressure should be used as a minimum. Note that these earth pressures only apply to gravity and semi-gravity cantilever walls.
key_points: Minimum equivalent fluid weight of 4.8 kN/m^3 (30 pcf) per AASHTO Standard Specifications
If calculated earth pressures are lower than equivalent fluid weight, use the equivalent fluid pressure as a minimum
Equivalent fluid method applies to gravity and semi-gravity cantilever walls only
sections.applicability: Establishing minimum lateral earth pressure for gravity and semi-gravity cantilever wall design.

sections.title: Live Load Surcharge
sections.body: If live loads (traffic) can occur within a horizontal distance behind the top of a wall or abutment wall equal to one-half of the wall height (measured from the heel of the footing), the lateral load for design should be increased to account for the additional lateral earth pressure that will act on the wall. The live load surcharge is estimated as an equivalent soil surcharge behind the wall or abutment. However, if there is an approach slab, the live loads are applied to the corbel on the abutment backwall. The equivalent height of soil to use in calculating the live load surcharge is 0.6 m (2 ft). The unit weight for this imaginary surcharge is typically taken as 19.6 kN/m^3 (125 pcf). The pressure distribution from this equivalent soil height is uniform along the back of the wall, and the resultant is halfway up from the base of the wall. The lateral load due to live load surcharge is then calculated as: P_LS = K * gamma' * h_eq * H (Equation 6-5), where P_LS is the lateral load due to live load surcharge per unit length, K is the lateral earth pressure coefficient (K_o or K_a), gamma' is the effective unit weight, h_eq is the equivalent height of soil surcharge (0.6 m), and H is the height of retained backfill.
key_points: Live load surcharge applies when traffic is within horizontal distance of 0.5H behind the wall
If approach slab is present, live loads are applied to the corbel on the abutment backwall instead
Equivalent surcharge height h_eq = 0.6 m (2 ft) with unit weight of 19.6 kN/m^3 (125 pcf)
Surcharge pressure distribution is uniform along the wall, with resultant at H/2 from base
P_LS = K * gamma' * h_eq * H
equations: Equation 6-5: P_LS = K * gamma' * h_eq * H (lateral load due to live load surcharge per unit length)
figures: Figure 6-3: Lateral Earth Pressures on Abutments
sections.applicability: Computing additional lateral load from traffic surcharge on abutment walls.

sections.title: Sizing the Footing
sections.body: Once all the loads acting on the footing have been calculated, the footing should be sized such that: (1) the footing is stable under eccentrically applied loads (i.e., the footing will not overturn) and such that negative contact stress does not develop beneath the footing (soil cannot transfer tensile stress), determined by computing the effective footing dimensions (Section 6.4.1); (2) the maximum applied bearing stress is less than the allowable bearing capacity, considering the potential for both shear failure and settlement, determined using the effective footing area and comparing it with the calculated allowable bearing capacity (Section 6.4.2); and (3) the footing will not slide due to lateral loads (Section 6.4.3).
key_points: Three sizing criteria: overturning stability, allowable bearing capacity, and sliding resistance
Footing must not develop negative (tensile) contact stress beneath it
Effective footing dimensions used for eccentricity and bearing stress calculations
Maximum applied bearing stress must be less than allowable bearing capacity (shear failure and settlement)
Sliding stability must be checked against lateral loads
sections.applicability: Overview of the three criteria governing footing size selection for bridge foundations.

sections.title: Effective Footing Dimensions and Overturning Stability
sections.body: Eccentric loading occurs when a footing is subjected to a combination of vertical loads and moments, or moments induced by shear loads transferred to the footing. Abutments and retaining wall footings are examples of footings subjected to this type of load condition. Moments can also be applied to interior column footings due to skewed superstructures, impact loads from vessels or ice, seismic loads or loading in any sort of continuous frame. The effect of the eccentric load is to distribute the load over a smaller area than the entire footing area. The eccentricity correction is usually applied by reducing the width (B_f) and length (L_f) such that: B'_f = B_f - 2*e_B (Equation 6-6), L'_f = L_f - 2*e_L (Equation 6-7), where e_B and e_L are the eccentric distances in the B_f and L_f directions, respectively, computed by dividing the applied moment by the applied vertical load. The reduced footing dimensions B'_f and L'_f are termed the effective footing dimensions. When eccentric load occurs in both directions, the bearing pressure is assumed to act over a fictitious area: A' = B'_f * L'_f (Equation 6-8). Note that the concept of effective footing dimensions and area is an approximation made to account for eccentric loading and is not representative of the actual stress distribution under a footing subjected to eccentric loads. Structural design of the footing is performed using trapezoidal or triangular stress distributions that more conservatively model the stress distribution under an eccentrically loaded footing as described in Section 6.6. Footings on soil should be designed such that the eccentricity in any direction (e_B or e_L) is less than one-sixth (1/6) of the actual footing dimension in the same direction to ensure that zero contact pressure does not exist beneath the footing (AASHTO, 1996). For footings on rock, the eccentricity should be less than one-fourth (1/4) of the actual footing dimension. If the eccentricity does not exceed these limits, separate calculation for stability with respect to overturning need not be performed.
key_points: Effective footing dimensions account for eccentric loading: B'_f = B_f - 2*e_B, L'_f = L_f - 2*e_L
Eccentricity e = M / V (moment divided by vertical load) in each direction
Effective area A' = B'_f * L'_f used for bearing stress calculation with uniform pressure assumption
Eccentricity on soil must be < B/6 or L/6 to avoid zero contact pressure (AASHTO 1996)
Eccentricity on rock must be < B/4 or L/4
If eccentricity within these limits, separate overturning calculation is not needed
Effective dimensions are an approximation; structural design uses actual trapezoidal/triangular distributions
equations: Equation 6-8: A' = B'_f * L'_f (effective footing area)
figures: Figure 6-4: Notations for Footings Subjected to Eccentric, Inclined Loads (after Kulhawy, 1983)
Figure 6-5: Eccentrically Loaded Footing with (a) Linear Pressure Distribution (Structural Design) and (b) Equivalent Uniform Pressure Distribution (Sizing the Footing)
sections.applicability: Computing effective footing dimensions for eccentric loading and checking overturning stability.

sections.title: Allowable Bearing Stress
sections.body: Using the procedures in Sections 5.2 and 5.3, an allowable bearing capacity should be computed that provides a minimum factor of safety of 3.0 against bearing failure in shear and limits the settlement of the footing to a tolerable amount. It is typically convenient to present the allowable bearing capacity as a range of bearing stresses plotted as a function of effective footing widths. Alternatively, settlements could be computed and tabulated for a variety of applied stresses and footing widths. An acceptable footing design may be obtained by sizing the footing such that the applied bearing stress over the effective footing area A', assuming a rectangular pressure distribution, is less than the allowable bearing pressure computed using the procedures in Chapter 5. Because the pressure distribution is assumed to be uniform, B_f in Equation 5-14 may be replaced by B'_f.
key_points: Minimum factor of safety of 3.0 against bearing failure in shear
Settlement must be limited to a tolerable amount
Allowable bearing capacity conveniently presented as stress vs. effective footing width
Applied bearing stress = Q / A' (load over effective area with uniform rectangular distribution)
Use effective width B'_f in place of B_f in bearing capacity equations
Settlements can alternatively be tabulated for a range of applied stresses and footing widths
sections.applicability: Determining allowable bearing stress and comparing with applied stress for footing sizing.

sections.title: Sliding
sections.body: The loads that act laterally on the footing should be compared to the allowable sliding resistance computed according to the procedures in Section 5.4. If the computed factor of safety is less than 1.5, the footing width should be increased. Addition of a key may also be considered, keeping in mind the limitations of key construction and effectiveness described in Section 5.4.
key_points: Compare lateral loads to allowable sliding resistance from Section 5.4
Minimum factor of safety of 1.5 for sliding stability
Increase footing width if FOS < 1.5
Addition of a shear key is an alternative, but consider construction limitations and effectiveness
sections.applicability: Checking sliding stability of bridge shallow foundations under lateral loads.

sections.title: Design of Shallow Foundations for Infrequent Transient Loads
sections.body: Bridge design may need to include consideration of loading conditions that rarely, if ever, occur during the life of the structure. Some of these load conditions can impose large loads on the structure and the foundations. Examples of loads that may impact bridge design include ice load, wind load, vessel impact and, notably, earthquake or seismic loads. These large loads can control the design and size of a foundation. The performance objective of the structure, and therefore the foundations, should be selected before establishing the design criteria. It may be considered that structural collapse is not acceptable, but that some structural damage is tolerable if one of these transient loads is applied to the structure. The concept of allowable bearing capacity that includes consideration of limiting both bearing failure in shear and settlement does not lend itself to design for infrequent transient loads. If some structural damage, but no collapse, is considered an acceptable result from the application of such a load, it is not reasonable to design the foundations for total settlement limited to, say, 25 mm (1 in). When considering infrequent transient loads, Service Load Design provisions include an allowance for overstress above the allowable capacity of a member. For soils, however, the 125 to 150 percent overstress allowance means that there is still a factor of safety against a collapse (bearing failure in shear) of at least 2.0. One step in this process is AASHTO's adoption of the Load and Resistance Factor Design (LRFD) methodology (AASHTO, 1998), which includes provisions for considering the performance of a structure under typical, or service loads, that are generally controlled by deflection (e.g., settlement), and strength or extreme event loads that may be controlled by the ultimate strength of a material (e.g., ultimate bearing capacity). Further discussion of the LRFD method as applied to shallow foundations is included in Appendix C.
key_points: Infrequent transient loads include ice, wind, vessel impact, earthquake/seismic loads
Performance objectives should allow some structural damage without collapse for transient loads
Traditional allowable bearing capacity (shear + settlement) approach is not well suited for infrequent loads
Service Load Design allows 125-150% overstress for transient loads, still maintaining FOS >= 2.0 against shear failure
LRFD methodology separates service loads (settlement-controlled) from strength/extreme event loads (capacity-controlled)
LRFD discussion for shallow foundations included in Appendix C
sections.applicability: Designing bridge shallow foundations for infrequent transient loads such as seismic, vessel impact, wind, and ice.

sections.title: Soil-Structure Interaction Analyses and Shallow Foundation Stiffness
sections.body: An additional consideration for shallow foundations designed to resist large, transient loads is the effect of soil-structure interaction. The loads calculated for a structure subjected to a large transient load will depend on how the structure responds to the application of the load. The structure response is, in turn, dependent on the stiffness of the foundation and the foundation soils. An accurate prediction of the loads will depend on an accurate prediction of the foundation stiffness. Of particular interest to designers is the response of foundations to transient lateral loads, such as those applied by seismic loads or vessel impact. For shallow foundations, the foundation stiffness will therefore be a function of the shear modulus and Poisson's ratio of the soil. A detailed description of evaluating soil and foundation stiffnesses is not included here. The reader is referred to GEC No. 3: Geotechnical Earthquake Engineering for Highways (Kavazanjian et al., 1997) and the course materials and design examples developed for National Highway Institute's Seismic Design of Bridges (Mast et al., 1996) for guidance on calculating foundation loads due to transient lateral forces.
key_points: Soil-structure interaction affects loads calculated for structures under large transient loads
Foundation stiffness depends on the shear modulus and Poisson's ratio of the soil
Accurate load prediction requires accurate foundation stiffness prediction
Foundation response to transient lateral loads (seismic, vessel impact) is of particular interest
Refer to GEC No. 3 and NHI Seismic Design of Bridges for detailed guidance
sections.applicability: Considering soil-structure interaction effects on foundation loads from transient lateral loading.

sections.title: Structural Design of the Footing
sections.body: The contact pressure beneath a spread footing is, in reality, a function of the stiffness of the footing and the compressibility and strength of the soil. However, the most common practical approach is to assume that the footing is rigid with a linear distribution of contact pressure. This results in either a trapezoidal or triangular shaped contact pressure distribution, as shown in Figure 6-6. The maximum and minimum pressures beneath the footing can be computed using Equations 6-9 through 6-13. For e_L <= L_f/6: q_max = Q[1 + 6(e_L/L_f)] / (B_f * L_f) (Equation 6-9), q_min = Q[1 - 6(e_L/L_f)] / (B_f * L_f) (Equation 6-10). For L_f/6 < e_L < L_f/2: q_max = 2Q / (3*B_f*[(L_f/2) - e_L]) (Equation 6-11), q_min = 0 (Equation 6-12), L_1 = 3[(L_f/2) - e_L] (Equation 6-13), where L_1 is the length of the triangular-shaped contact pressure distribution. Note: When the eccentricity is in the B_f direction, the minimum and maximum contact pressures are computed with Equations 6-9 through 6-13 by replacing e_L with e_B, L_f with B_f, and B_f with L_f. The structural design of the footing should then be performed in accordance with Section 8 of the AASHTO Standard Specifications (1996). The soil pressures used for this design are the customary trapezoidal or triangular pressures shown in Figure 6-6 and calculated using Equations 6-9 through 6-13, not the equivalent uniform rectangular pressures used to size the footing dimensions. The following failure modes should be considered during structural design of the footing: consider the moment in the footing as a function of the column connection (pinned, fixed or sliding, equivalent rectangular column); increase moment (flexural) steel in the short direction per AASHTO Standard Specifications (1996); when compression is induced at the face of the column, investigate shear at 'd' away from the column face in compression (where 'd' is the full depth of the footing), and if tension is induced, investigate shear at the face of the column; consider punching or two-way shear around the column. For abutments, each structural element is designed similar to spread footings, with the backwall and stem wall designed for the design soil pressures. Wingwalls, if included, are designed for the maximum soil pressures, and the connection of the wingwall to the stem wall is critical so that it will not fracture.
key_points: Assume rigid footing with linear contact pressure distribution (trapezoidal or triangular)
For e_L <= L_f/6: trapezoidal distribution with q_max and q_min computed from Equations 6-9 and 6-10
For L_f/6 < e_L < L_f/2: triangular distribution with q_min = 0 and L_1 = 3[(L_f/2) - e_L]
Use actual trapezoidal/triangular pressures for structural design, NOT the equivalent uniform pressure used for sizing
Structural design per AASHTO Standard Specifications Section 8
Check: moment at column face, flexural steel in short direction, one-way shear at 'd' from column face, and punching (two-way) shear
Abutment elements designed similarly; wingwall-to-stemwall connection is critical to prevent fracture
equations: Equation 6-9: q_max = Q[1 + 6(e_L/L_f)] / (B_f * L_f) (for e_L <= L_f/6)
Equation 6-10: q_min = Q[1 - 6(e_L/L_f)] / (B_f * L_f) (for e_L <= L_f/6)
Equation 6-11: q_max = 2Q / (3*B_f*[(L_f/2) - e_L]) (for L_f/6 < e_L < L_f/2)
Equation 6-13: L_1 = 3[(L_f/2) - e_L] (length of triangular contact pressure distribution)
figures: Figure 6-6: Contact Pressure for Footing Loaded Eccentrically About One Axis: (a) for e_L <= L_f/6, and (b) for L_f/6 < e_L < L_f/2 (AASHTO, 1996)
sections.applicability: Structural design of bridge spread footings using trapezoidal or triangular contact pressure distributions for reinforcement and shear checks.
